romania.title: Voyager 1, la o zi-lumină de Pământ. Imaginile spectaculoase cu Jupiter care au schimbat ce știm despre Sistemul Solar
romania.summary: Sonda Voyager 1 a NASA, lansată în 1977, urmează să atingă miercuri, 18 noiembrie, o distanță record de 25,89 miliarde de kilometri față de Pământ. Cu aproape cinci decenii în urmă, imaginile realizate de sondă în timpul explorării planetei Jupiter au dezvăluit o atmosferă mult mai dinamică decât se credea, existența unui sistem de inele și activitatea vulcanică de pe satelitul Io, schimbând radical cunoștințele astronomilor despre Sistemul Solar.

romania.title: Primele semne ale bolii Alzheimer ar putea apărea în afara creierului. Descoperirea surprinzătoare a cercetătorilor
romania.summary: Primele semne ale bolii Alzheimer ar putea apărea în afara creierului, cu mult înainte ca problemele de memorie să devină evidente. Cercetătorii de la Universitatea Central Florida, din Statele Unite, au descoperit că anumite mutații genetice asociate bolii pot afecta direct comunicarea dintre nervi și mușchi. Descoperirea ar putea explica de ce unele persoane dezvoltă dificultăți de mers, echilibru și coordonare înainte de apariția simptomelor cognitive, relatează ScienceDaily.

medical.title: New study finds weight stigma may keep young adults from seeking medical care
medical.summary: New research from the University of Minnesota Medical School highlights how weight stigma in health care settings may prevent young adults from seeking medical care, particularly those experiencing severe disordered eating behaviors.

medical.title: Scientists tracked kids for 8 years. What they found about screen time was surprising
medical.summary: A surprising Finnish study found that children who spent more time using screens tended to have better cognitive processing abilities as teenagers, challenging the assumption that screen time is always harmful. Researchers suggest that what children do on screens may matter more than how much time they spend using them.

medical.title: Middle-aged and older adults favor TV and YouTube for home exercise, survey finds
medical.summary: As populations continue to age, creating environments that enable individuals to incorporate regular physical activity into their daily lives is essential for maintaining health and functional independence. Smartphone applications and video-based programs are increasingly being used to support home-based exercise. However, relatively little is known about the types of exercise support and digital media that people prefer to use or whether these preferences differ according to age or residential area.

medical.title: The hidden language of psychopathy is not what scientists expected
medical.summary: Scientists have discovered that psychopathic traits are associated with surprisingly different patterns of language, with some individuals using more positive words and others expressing greater negativity or less anxiety. The findings challenge familiar stereotypes about psychopathy and suggest that the stories people tell about their lives may offer important clues about their personalities.

medical.title: Ozempic and Mounjaro may have a surprising effect on your brain
medical.summary: Blockbuster weight loss drugs like Ozempic and Mounjaro may do more than help people shed pounds, with growing evidence suggesting they could also influence brain health. Although studies have linked GLP-1 medications to a lower risk of dementia, major trials found that semaglutide did not slow Alzheimer's disease. Scientists suspect these drugs may be more effective at preserving memory and thinking abilities in people with obesity or diabetes, especially before cognitive problems appear.

medical.title: Doctors are raising concerns about US babies born with measles
medical.summary: For the first time in decades, U.S. doctors are sounding the alarm about babies coming into the world with measles.

medical.title: Viruses in the gut microbiome linked to irritable bowel syndrome
medical.summary: The human gut microbiome is home to a vast and largely unexplored world of viruses, which could hold important clues to how the gut ecosystem works.

medical.title: How radiation or chemotherapy before bone marrow transplantation may shape human immune system recovery
medical.summary: In a new study from the USC Stem Cell lab of Rong Lu, Ph.D., researchers used genetic barcoding to track individual human blood-forming stem and progenitor cells after transplanting them into mice. The study revealed how different types of human blood-forming cells regenerate the blood and immune system, and how different forms of pretransplant conditioning, a treatment used to prepare a recipient before bone marrow transplantation, affected blood and immune cell recovery.

medical.title: Wine, beer, or spirits? Massive study reveals a surprising health divide
medical.summary: A massive study of more than 340,000 adults found that moderate wine drinkers had a 21% lower risk of cardiovascular death, while even light consumption of beer, cider, or spirits was linked to increased risk. Although heavy drinking was harmful regardless of beverage type, the findings suggest that the relationship between alcohol and health may be more complicated than previously thought.

medical.title: US flu cases edge up as virus claims lives of two children
medical.summary: Although U.S. cases of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and COVID-19 are low, the proportion of outpatient visits for influenza-like illness (ILI) is 3.2%, above the 2.9% national baseline, indicating the beginning of flu season in earnest.

medical.title: Cannabis addiction linked to 57% higher odds of suicidal thoughts
medical.summary: A massive study involving more than 415,000 Americans has uncovered a concerning connection between cannabis use disorder and suicidal thoughts. Researchers found that adults with the disorder had 57% higher odds of experiencing suicidal thoughts, with women and younger adults facing particularly elevated risks.

medical.title: Scientists discover a common sugar may help cancer cells break free and spread
medical.summary: Scientists have uncovered a surprising way that fructose, a sugar commonly found in sweetened foods and drinks, may help aggressive ovarian cancer spread. Researchers discovered that cancer cells surviving chemotherapy release fructose that weakens the bonds holding neighboring tumor cells together, making it easier for cancer to spread. High dietary fructose levels and cholesterol-lowering statins also produced concerning effects in preclinical experiments.

medical.title: Walking and weight training may not be enough to keep your bones strong
medical.summary: A surprising new study suggests that walking, jogging, and even traditional weight training may be less effective at stimulating bone formation than high-intensity sports involving explosive movements and sudden changes in direction. Researchers found that activities such as football and handball increased markers of bone formation by up to 46%, potentially revealing a better way to protect bones against aging and osteoporosis.

science.title: Why some shoppers skip coupons—even when they offer a deal
science.summary: Coupons promise savings, but not every shopper sees them as clear-cut bargains. For some consumers, such discounts may lead them to ask, "Where's the catch?"

science.title: A mysterious twist in the universe’s oldest light could reveal new physics
science.summary: Scientists have spotted hints of a mysterious rotation in the universe’s oldest light that could reveal new physics and shed light on dark matter and dark energy. A new technique developed at UC San Diego could help rule out misleading telescope errors, bringing researchers closer to determining whether the strange signal is real.

science.title: DESI weighs the Milky Way more precisely than ever
science.summary: To estimate the Milky Way's mass, astronomers need to track the movements of stars and smaller satellite galaxies under its gravitational pull. The faster these objects travel at a given distance, the more mass is needed to hold them in place. For some time, these measurements have shown that most of our galaxy's mass can't be accounted for by the stars and gas we can see. However, they have also produced estimates that differ widely.

science.title: Japan space probe changes target over engine trouble
science.summary: A Japanese probe that returned precious asteroid dust to Earth six years ago has changed course in its extended mission, officials said Tuesday, citing issues in its aging engines.

science.title: Humpback whale snot unlocks whole-genome sequencing without invasive sampling
science.summary: New research from the University of St Andrews, in collaboration with the University of Copenhagen, the North Coast Cetacean Society and Fisheries and Oceans Canada, has sequenced a whole whale genome using samples of "whale snot" collected by small drones off the coast of British Columbia—a world first.

science.title: Tossing Fireworks from Cloud to Cloud
science.summary: For many astronauts, the spectacular sight of lightning stands out when looking back at Earth from the International Space Station.

science.title: What makes food 'organic?' For many consumers, the answer isn't always on the label
science.summary: "Organic" is a word we encounter every time we visit the supermarket. It's also one that can mean very different things to different people.

science.title: A material just one atom thick reveals a strange quantum secret
science.summary: Researchers at the University of Osaka have discovered a remarkable quantum state forming at the boundary between a one-atom-thick material and a metal. They observed electrons behaving as though they were unusually heavy, including a previously unseen state created by interactions between the ultrathin layer and the copper beneath it. This first-of-its-kind observation reveals a promising new way to control exotic quantum behavior.

science.title: A massive new simulation reveals how the universe emerged from darkness
science.summary: A groundbreaking new supercomputer simulation is revealing how the universe escaped its cosmic dark age and transformed into a cosmos filled with stars and galaxies. Called Lumina, it recreates 2 billion years of early cosmic history across a region 1.6 billion light-years wide, capturing extraordinary details that previous simulations could not.

science.title: NASA’s Parker Solar Probe discovers a hidden pattern in the Sun’s chaotic magnetic fields
science.summary: NASA’s Parker Solar Probe has revealed a surprising secret hidden within the chaos of space: turbulent magnetic fields reverse their direction of rotation when examined at extremely small scales. The discovery exposes an unexpected pattern in solar wind turbulence that could help scientists better understand solar activity and predict geomagnetic storms.

science.title: Scientists discover that necks didn't evolve for the reason we thought
science.summary: Scientists have discovered that the first animals to venture onto land nearly 380 million years ago had surprisingly stiff necks, overturning a long-standing theory about evolution. Rather than evolving to help animals turn their heads, necks may have emerged as part of the anatomical changes that allowed them to move using their front limbs.

environment.summary: A Swedish compensation scheme designed to encourage coexistence between reindeer herders and carnivores is facing growing criticism from Indigenous Sámi communities. environment.summary: Hafsa Begum, 25, spent most of her recent pregnancy in a two-room apartment on the third floor of a five-storey building in a densely populated neighborhood of Dhaka, Bangladesh. Her bedroom remained dark even during the day, she says, as neighboring residential buildings blocked sunlight and restricted the flow of fresh air through the windows. […]

environment.title: Fossil of extinct giant bird discovered in Flores cave, Indonesia
environment.summary: Archaeologists excavating Liang Bua cave on the Indonesian island of Flores have identified a new species of extinct giant bird that roamed the region some 150,000 years ago, according to a recent study. The giant bird was a kind of megapode — large, chicken-like birds that today live in the broader Australasian region. These birds […]

environment.title: Scientists just found dinosaur blood that survived 115 million years
environment.summary: Scientists have discovered chemically confirmed traces of ancient blood inside 115-million-year-old dinosaur bones, challenging assumptions about how long biological molecules can survive. The extraordinary preservation could unlock new clues about dinosaur physiology and even help scientists search for ancient life elsewhere in the universe.

environment.title: The Great Barrier Reef's most notorious coral killer may actually be helping it
environment.summary: Crown-of-thorns starfish are notorious for devouring coral reefs, but surprising new research reveals these spiny predators may actually help reefs thrive when their populations are kept in check. Scientists studying Australia's Great Barrier Reef discovered that nearly 75% of observed starfish feeding events left behind living coral tissue, rather than destroying entire colonies. By feeding on fast-growing, dominant corals, the starfish create opportunities for slower-growing species to survive, potentially increasing coral biodiversity.

environment.title: Ancient ape fossil in Egypt could rewrite the story of human origins
environment.summary: A 17- to 18-million-year-old ape fossil discovered in Egypt is challenging long-held beliefs about where the ancestors of humans and other modern apes first evolved. Scientists now suspect that North Africa and the Middle East, rather than East Africa, may have been the cradle of modern ape evolution.

environment.title: Scientists discover the hidden “muscles” trees use to straighten themselves
environment.summary: Scientists have discovered that trees can sense their own shape and straighten their trunks using specialized wood that acts like opposing muscles. This remarkable ability helps trees maintain their posture and could lead to stronger forests, better timber, and more resilient crops.

environment.title: Do spiders dream? Scientists just found a surprising clue
environment.summary: Scientists have discovered that spiders may sleep in ways surprisingly similar to humans, complete with distinct sleep stages and a dream-like REM state. Researchers at the University of Bonn studied the Australian jumping spider Portia fimbriata, a remarkably clever hunter known for its sophisticated strategies. By recording the spiders over several days and nights, they found clear evidence of regulated sleep, including a REM-like stage marked by eye movements and muscle twitches.

environment.title: 1.9-million-year-old discovery rewrites the story of human evolution
environment.summary: New evidence suggests that early humans reached the Jordan Valley at least 1.9 million years ago, hundreds of thousands of years earlier than scientists previously thought. Advanced dating methods revealed that the ‘Ubeidiya site is roughly as old as the famous Dmanisi site in Georgia, placing both among the earliest known human settlements outside Africa.

mix_items.title: Primele semne ale bolii Alzheimer ar putea apărea în afara creierului. Descoperirea surprinzătoare a cercetătorilor
mix_items.summary: Primele semne ale bolii Alzheimer ar putea apărea în afara creierului, cu mult înainte ca problemele de memorie să devină evidente. Cercetătorii de la Universitatea Central Florida, din Statele Unite, au descoperit că anumite mutații genetice asociate bolii pot afecta direct comunicarea dintre nervi și mușchi. Descoperirea ar putea explica de ce unele persoane dezvoltă dificultăți de mers, echilibru și coordonare înainte de apariția simptomelor cognitive, relatează ScienceDaily.

mix_items.summary: Când medicii au anunţat, pe 13 octombrie, că papa Leon al XIV-lea suferea de cancer pulmonar, mai mulţi oficiali de la Vatican au speculat că diagnosticul îl va obliga pe liderul catolic să anuleze turneul de 12 zile planificat în America de Sud şi, în general, să-şi reducă ritmul călătoriilor, scrie Reuters.

mix_items.summary: New research from the University of Minnesota Medical School highlights how weight stigma in health care settings may prevent young adults from seeking medical care, particularly those experiencing severe disordered eating behaviors.

mix_items.title: A mysterious twist in the universe’s oldest light could reveal new physics
mix_items.summary: Scientists have spotted hints of a mysterious rotation in the universe’s oldest light that could reveal new physics and shed light on dark matter and dark energy. A new technique developed at UC San Diego could help rule out misleading telescope errors, bringing researchers closer to determining whether the strange signal is real.

mix_items.title: Scientists tracked kids for 8 years. What they found about screen time was surprising
mix_items.summary: A surprising Finnish study found that children who spent more time using screens tended to have better cognitive processing abilities as teenagers, challenging the assumption that screen time is always harmful. Researchers suggest that what children do on screens may matter more than how much time they spend using them.

mix_items.title: Middle-aged and older adults favor TV and YouTube for home exercise, survey finds
mix_items.summary: As populations continue to age, creating environments that enable individuals to incorporate regular physical activity into their daily lives is essential for maintaining health and functional independence. Smartphone applications and video-based programs are increasingly being used to support home-based exercise. However, relatively little is known about the types of exercise support and digital media that people prefer to use or whether these preferences differ according to age or residential area.

mix_items.title: DESI weighs the Milky Way more precisely than ever
mix_items.summary: To estimate the Milky Way's mass, astronomers need to track the movements of stars and smaller satellite galaxies under its gravitational pull. The faster these objects travel at a given distance, the more mass is needed to hold them in place. For some time, these measurements have shown that most of our galaxy's mass can't be accounted for by the stars and gas we can see. However, they have also produced estimates that differ widely.

mix_items.title: The hidden language of psychopathy is not what scientists expected
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered that psychopathic traits are associated with surprisingly different patterns of language, with some individuals using more positive words and others expressing greater negativity or less anxiety. The findings challenge familiar stereotypes about psychopathy and suggest that the stories people tell about their lives may offer important clues about their personalities.

mix_items.title: Ozempic and Mounjaro may have a surprising effect on your brain
mix_items.summary: Blockbuster weight loss drugs like Ozempic and Mounjaro may do more than help people shed pounds, with growing evidence suggesting they could also influence brain health. Although studies have linked GLP-1 medications to a lower risk of dementia, major trials found that semaglutide did not slow Alzheimer's disease. Scientists suspect these drugs may be more effective at preserving memory and thinking abilities in people with obesity or diabetes, especially before cognitive problems appear.

mix_items.title: Japan space probe changes target over engine trouble
mix_items.summary: A Japanese probe that returned precious asteroid dust to Earth six years ago has changed course in its extended mission, officials said Tuesday, citing issues in its aging engines.

mix_items.title: Doctors are raising concerns about US babies born with measles
mix_items.summary: For the first time in decades, U.S. doctors are sounding the alarm about babies coming into the world with measles.

mix_items.title: Viruses in the gut microbiome linked to irritable bowel syndrome
mix_items.summary: The human gut microbiome is home to a vast and largely unexplored world of viruses, which could hold important clues to how the gut ecosystem works.

mix_items.title: Humpback whale snot unlocks whole-genome sequencing without invasive sampling
mix_items.summary: New research from the University of St Andrews, in collaboration with the University of Copenhagen, the North Coast Cetacean Society and Fisheries and Oceans Canada, has sequenced a whole whale genome using samples of "whale snot" collected by small drones off the coast of British Columbia—a world first.

mix_items.title: How radiation or chemotherapy before bone marrow transplantation may shape human immune system recovery
mix_items.summary: In a new study from the USC Stem Cell lab of Rong Lu, Ph.D., researchers used genetic barcoding to track individual human blood-forming stem and progenitor cells after transplanting them into mice. The study revealed how different types of human blood-forming cells regenerate the blood and immune system, and how different forms of pretransplant conditioning, a treatment used to prepare a recipient before bone marrow transplantation, affected blood and immune cell recovery.

mix_items.summary: For many astronauts, the spectacular sight of lightning stands out when looking back at Earth from the International Space Station.

mix_items.title: Wine, beer, or spirits? Massive study reveals a surprising health divide
mix_items.summary: A massive study of more than 340,000 adults found that moderate wine drinkers had a 21% lower risk of cardiovascular death, while even light consumption of beer, cider, or spirits was linked to increased risk. Although heavy drinking was harmful regardless of beverage type, the findings suggest that the relationship between alcohol and health may be more complicated than previously thought.

mix_items.title: What makes food 'organic?' For many consumers, the answer isn't always on the label
mix_items.summary: "Organic" is a word we encounter every time we visit the supermarket. It's also one that can mean very different things to different people.

mix_items.title: US flu cases edge up as virus claims lives of two children
mix_items.summary: Although U.S. cases of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and COVID-19 are low, the proportion of outpatient visits for influenza-like illness (ILI) is 3.2%, above the 2.9% national baseline, indicating the beginning of flu season in earnest.

mix_items.title: Cannabis addiction linked to 57% higher odds of suicidal thoughts
mix_items.summary: A massive study involving more than 415,000 Americans has uncovered a concerning connection between cannabis use disorder and suicidal thoughts. Researchers found that adults with the disorder had 57% higher odds of experiencing suicidal thoughts, with women and younger adults facing particularly elevated risks.

mix_items.title: A material just one atom thick reveals a strange quantum secret
mix_items.summary: Researchers at the University of Osaka have discovered a remarkable quantum state forming at the boundary between a one-atom-thick material and a metal. They observed electrons behaving as though they were unusually heavy, including a previously unseen state created by interactions between the ultrathin layer and the copper beneath it. This first-of-its-kind observation reveals a promising new way to control exotic quantum behavior.

mix_items.summary: A Swedish compensation scheme designed to encourage coexistence between reindeer herders and carnivores is facing growing criticism from Indigenous Sámi communities. Inadequate payments, deficient monitoring methods and lack of meaningful dialogue between authorities and reindeer herders are eroding trust in the system, researchers tell Mongabay. “The state of Sweden hasn’t actually understood how severe and […]

The film detailed their lives while free on bail awaiting a likely guilty verdict for “plotting against the government” by fighting to protect Cambodia’s natural […]

mix_items.title: Rising preterm births in Bangladesh linked to extreme heat, research suggests
mix_items.summary: Hafsa Begum, 25, spent most of her recent pregnancy in a two-room apartment on the third floor of a five-storey building in a densely populated neighborhood of Dhaka, Bangladesh. Her bedroom remained dark even during the day, she says, as neighboring residential buildings blocked sunlight and restricted the flow of fresh air through the windows. […]

mix_items.title: Fossil of extinct giant bird discovered in Flores cave, Indonesia
mix_items.summary: Archaeologists excavating Liang Bua cave on the Indonesian island of Flores have identified a new species of extinct giant bird that roamed the region some 150,000 years ago, according to a recent study. The giant bird was a kind of megapode — large, chicken-like birds that today live in the broader Australasian region. These birds […]

mix_items.title: Scientists discover a common sugar may help cancer cells break free and spread
mix_items.summary: Scientists have uncovered a surprising way that fructose, a sugar commonly found in sweetened foods and drinks, may help aggressive ovarian cancer spread. Researchers discovered that cancer cells surviving chemotherapy release fructose that weakens the bonds holding neighboring tumor cells together, making it easier for cancer to spread. High dietary fructose levels and cholesterol-lowering statins also produced concerning effects in preclinical experiments.

mix_items.title: A massive new simulation reveals how the universe emerged from darkness
mix_items.summary: A groundbreaking new supercomputer simulation is revealing how the universe escaped its cosmic dark age and transformed into a cosmos filled with stars and galaxies. Called Lumina, it recreates 2 billion years of early cosmic history across a region 1.6 billion light-years wide, capturing extraordinary details that previous simulations could not.

mix_items.title: NASA’s Parker Solar Probe discovers a hidden pattern in the Sun’s chaotic magnetic fields
mix_items.summary: NASA’s Parker Solar Probe has revealed a surprising secret hidden within the chaos of space: turbulent magnetic fields reverse their direction of rotation when examined at extremely small scales. The discovery exposes an unexpected pattern in solar wind turbulence that could help scientists better understand solar activity and predict geomagnetic storms.

mix_items.title: Walking and weight training may not be enough to keep your bones strong
mix_items.summary: A surprising new study suggests that walking, jogging, and even traditional weight training may be less effective at stimulating bone formation than high-intensity sports involving explosive movements and sudden changes in direction. Researchers found that activities such as football and handball increased markers of bone formation by up to 46%, potentially revealing a better way to protect bones against aging and osteoporosis.

mix_items.title: Scientists discover that necks didn't evolve for the reason we thought
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered that the first animals to venture onto land nearly 380 million years ago had surprisingly stiff necks, overturning a long-standing theory about evolution. Rather than evolving to help animals turn their heads, necks may have emerged as part of the anatomical changes that allowed them to move using their front limbs.

mix_items.title: Scientists just found dinosaur blood that survived 115 million years
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered chemically confirmed traces of ancient blood inside 115-million-year-old dinosaur bones, challenging assumptions about how long biological molecules can survive. The extraordinary preservation could unlock new clues about dinosaur physiology and even help scientists search for ancient life elsewhere in the universe.

mix_items.title: The Great Barrier Reef's most notorious coral killer may actually be helping it
mix_items.summary: Crown-of-thorns starfish are notorious for devouring coral reefs, but surprising new research reveals these spiny predators may actually help reefs thrive when their populations are kept in check. Scientists studying Australia's Great Barrier Reef discovered that nearly 75% of observed starfish feeding events left behind living coral tissue, rather than destroying entire colonies. By feeding on fast-growing, dominant corals, the starfish create opportunities for slower-growing species to survive, potentially increasing coral biodiversity.

mix_items.title: Ancient ape fossil in Egypt could rewrite the story of human origins
mix_items.summary: A 17- to 18-million-year-old ape fossil discovered in Egypt is challenging long-held beliefs about where the ancestors of humans and other modern apes first evolved. Scientists now suspect that North Africa and the Middle East, rather than East Africa, may have been the cradle of modern ape evolution.

mix_items.title: Scientists discover the hidden “muscles” trees use to straighten themselves
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered that trees can sense their own shape and straighten their trunks using specialized wood that acts like opposing muscles. This remarkable ability helps trees maintain their posture and could lead to stronger forests, better timber, and more resilient crops.

mix_items.title: Do spiders dream? Scientists just found a surprising clue
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered that spiders may sleep in ways surprisingly similar to humans, complete with distinct sleep stages and a dream-like REM state. Researchers at the University of Bonn studied the Australian jumping spider Portia fimbriata, a remarkably clever hunter known for its sophisticated strategies. By recording the spiders over several days and nights, they found clear evidence of regulated sleep, including a REM-like stage marked by eye movements and muscle twitches.

mix_items.title: 1.9-million-year-old discovery rewrites the story of human evolution
mix_items.summary: New evidence suggests that early humans reached the Jordan Valley at least 1.9 million years ago, hundreds of thousands of years earlier than scientists previously thought. Advanced dating methods revealed that the ‘Ubeidiya site is roughly as old as the famous Dmanisi site in Georgia, placing both among the earliest known human settlements outside Africa.
